desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

A block of consecutive nodes whose values add up to 0 can be deleted. Repeat the following until no block of consecutive nodes with sum 0 exists: take the leftmost node that is the first node of some zero-sum block, and delete the longest zero-sum block that starts at that node. Return the values of the remaining list.

For [1,2,-3,3,1] the leftmost block start is the head, where 1+2-3 = 0 is the longest zero-sum block, so it is deleted and the answer is [3,1] (deleting [-3,3] instead would give a different list, which is why the rule above fixes the order). For [1,2,3,-3,4] the answer is [1,2,4], and for [1,2,3,-3,-2] it is [1].

A node with value 0 is itself a zero-sum block of length one.
hints: A block of nodes from position i+1 to j has sum zero exactly when the prefix sums before i+1 and after j are equal.
Store prefix sums in a hash map. If a prefix sum repeats, everything between its two occurrences cancels. Which occurrence of the prefix value should you jump to to delete the longest block?

First pass: compute the prefix sum at every node (with a dummy node at prefix 0) and record in a map the last node having each prefix sum. Second pass: for every node in the chain from the dummy, set node.next = last[prefix(node)].next and move on to that next node.
editorial: Let P be the prefix sums of the list, with P = 0 before the head. A block of consecutive nodes sums to zero exactly when two prefix sums are equal. Deleting a zero-sum block does not change any later prefix sum, which is why the order described in the statement leads to the same result as a single sweep.

Pass one: walk the list from a dummy node and store, for each prefix sum, the last node where it occurs. Pass two: walk again with a running prefix sum, and for each node set its next to the node after last[prefix]. This jumps over the longest zero-sum block that begins right after the node. Afterwards no two kept boundaries share the same prefix sum, so no zero-sum block is left.
Time is O(n) and extra space is O(n) for the hash map. Repeating a naive search for a zero-sum block after each deletion would cost O(n<sup>2</sup>) or worse.
